name: Allopregnanolone
lead: Allopregnanolone (3alpha-hydroxy-5alpha-pregnan-20-one) is a neurosteroid the body makes from progesterone. It is a potent positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors in the brain.[1][2][3] Its levels rise in stress, the luteal phase and pregnancy, and fall after delivery.[4][5]

Its intravenous form, brexanolone, was approved by the US FDA in March 2019 for postpartum depression, the first neurosteroid approved; it was later withdrawn from the US market.[6][7] Oral analogs such as zuranolone followed.[8]
Allopregnanolone has no studied appearance use. Registered early-phase trials explore its use in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, traumatic brain injury and alcohol craving.[9][10][11][12]
infobox: Endogenous neurosteroid; GABA-A positive allosteric modulator

paras: The brain synthesises allopregnanolone in neurons and glia from progesterone through two enzymatic steps.[7][13] Experiments in rats showed that stress rapidly raises GABA-A-active steroids, and that levels and receptor plasticity shift in pregnancy and after delivery.[14][5] Researchers have linked altered levels to anxiety, depression and premenstrual conditions, and have reported that moderate increases can sometimes cause paradoxical irritability.[7][1]
Allopregnanolone binds two distinct transmembrane sites on GABA-A receptors and strengthens inhibitory currents.[3] Animal work also links it to changes in amygdala oscillatory states.[15]
Because oral bioavailability is low, therapeutic forms were given by infusion or developed as oral analogs. Its half-life is about 9 hours as brexanolone.[7]

Brexanolone was approved in March 2019 as a continuous infusion for postpartum depression. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, headache and dry mouth, and the product carried a REMS for excessive sedation.[7][6] Two phase 3 trials and an earlier controlled trial reported greater depression-score reductions than placebo.[6][16]

The compound was first identified in the 1930s during progesterone metabolism work, and its action on GABA-A receptors was described in the 1980s.[7][17] The late 1980s and 1990s saw a growing literature on neuroactive steroids.[17][1] Clinical development of neurosteroid drugs began in the 2000s and 2010s.[7]
Brexanolone is a controlled substance in the US. No community material on allopregnanolone was found for appearance use; any interest is in neurosteroids for mood, stress and sleep.

Two multicentre phase 3 trials of brexanolone in postpartum depression and an earlier randomised trial found larger reductions in depression ratings than placebo.[6][16] Small phase 1 and 2 studies registered for Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, traumatic brain injury and alcohol use disorder are exploratory.[9][10][11][12] No studies of allopregnanolone for appearance were found.

card.summary: Natural progesterone-derived neurosteroid behind the postpartum-depression drug brexanolone; no studied appearance use.
card.note: Poor oral bioavailability; approved form was an IV infusion since withdrawn from the US market.

quick.overview:
Allopregnanolone is a calming steroid made in the brain from progesterone. Its levels rise in pregnancy and drop after birth.

A synthetic IV version, brexanolone, was approved in 2019 for postpartum depression. Other uses remain in early trials, and no appearance use has been studied.
quick.mechanism: It boosts the effect of GABA at GABA-A receptors by binding to neurosteroid sites on the receptor, increasing inhibitory signalling.
quick.risks: Reported effects of the infused drug include sedation, dizziness, headache and dry mouth, with monitoring required. It is a controlled substance in the US, and is not available as a simple oral product because of low bioavailability.
